title: Xeodrifter™
text: Xenodrifter is a 2D watered down metroid clone- you know the kind. Navigate mazes, get power-ups to access new areas, fight evil space monsters, and backtracking galore. Xenodrifter straddles the gorge with one foot on the side of neat ideas with the other firmly planted in unnecessary tedium. The major power-up and mechanical theme is lifted from an older title Renagade Kid worked on called Mutant Mudds, where the protagonist can warp from foreground to background to traverse the world. Another major feature is how you can customize the gun- the hero's main form of attack. Want the bullets to weave through the air? There's an upgrade for that. Faster Bullets? Got it. Spray and pray? Right here. You can allocate points to make your gun as “wavy” or “fast” as you like. As you progress through the game, the more of these upgrade points you find and the crazier your custom gun becomes. However, the gameplay is fairly dull. The stages have bleak layouts with no real threats besides the odd off-screen enemy ramming you. The game just has that “autopilot” feel. Jump up ledges, stand still to shoot the bouncing baddy, move on. No real hazards, interesting enemies, or challenging puzzles. The bosses are the same creature with different colors and more attack actions. This visually makes bosses anti-climatic and their patterns obvious.  Oddly, the game feature few checkpoints- only one at the start of the stage and when you face the planet boss. This can lead to some false difficulty and more tedium as you face the same enemies, the same layout, with the same stage all over again from the beginning if you get nixed. Snore. If you absolutely enjoy these types of 2D action-adventure games then you've played much better and far worse. Xendrifter is in the middle- it has good bullet points to pique your interest, but nothing engaging to make you stay. If your interested in playing one of these types of games, Xenodrfter is not a good first choice. A nice second just to see what an “everyday” metroid-clone feels like. A sale, coupon, or bundle item- don't get it full price.

title: Xeodrifter™
text: I'm a fan of Bad Metroids, but man this one is pretty bad. Its most obvious sin is that it doesn't respect your time. After finishing a boss fight, you have to slog back through the level you just took a couple of tries to get through to reach the exit without save rooms or a (good) way to regain health. But that would be fine if the game were fundamentally fun, which this is not. I can't put it any better than describing the Eye Cube. The Eye Cube is an enemy that fires a big eye beam thing. This big eye beam cannot be dodged or avoided and takes up every available inch of the corridor. The only way to fight the Eye Cube is to stand past the extent of the beam and shoot from that point of safety, and the beam is so long that you can't actually see the Eye Cube. The Eye Cube dies after like 25 hits that you shoot blindly at an enemy off-screen. It is possibly the worst enemy I have ever seen in a video game. (For funzies, the hit box on the beam is substantially larger than the beam itself, like by the width of your character. But that is not the fundamental problem with the Eye Cube.) There's some bullet hell going on, but movement is floaty where it should be tight. There's a "jump to the background" mechanic, but the floor of the background doesn't quite line up with the floor of the foreground, and so you need to jump before you can pop back, but the difference between the minimum jump height and the maximum jump height is so slight that you jump into ceiling enemies in a way that's more or less out of your control. Every exploration item is misused. There's a jetpack, but you can't ever experience fun and freedom using the thing because the foreground camera is so close and there are milipedes everywhere. You get a dash mechanic, but the dash isn't long enough to avoid damage from the very irritating enemy that was introduced on the same map as the dash mechanic. There are stupid traps where you dash through a wall into a bullet from an off-screen enemy that activates only after you dash through the wall. It's short enough that you finish before you realize how much you hate this game, and I paid a dollar for it, so I'm not *really* complaining, but it's so bad. Oh and there's an ability you have to turn on and off several times per level. Instead of assigning a key to toggle it, you have to pause, navigate to it, turn it on, unpause, etc. Such a bad design choice.

title: Xeodrifter™
text: I was immediately interested in this game when I saw it was released by the same people who made Mutant Mudds. After watching the trailer for Xeodrifter, I was hoping to play a well-crafted action adventure game that hearkened back to the days of Metroid and Blaster Master. I'm happy to say that is exactly what I got. The premise of Xeodrifter is incredibly simple: your ship needs a new warp core and unless you want to be left stranded out in the depths of space forever, your only option is to explore four nearby planets and seach for a new core. As you explore each planet, you'll slowly uncover a plethora of health and weapon upgrades, as well as new abilties to help you on your way (rocket jump, submarine, etc.) There is no text in the game and that's okay: it helps immerse the player in the atmosphere of the game. That being said, the gameplay pulls through and makes Xeodrifter a fun play. While the controls are slightly floaty, the game moves at a nice pace. You have a selection of upgrades to choose from in upgrading your energy shot which allows for a little customization. As you uncover more and more upgrades, the difficulty of the game slowly ramps along with your progression. This, and the integration of your new abilties, keeps Xeodrifter from becoming boring or repetitive; as the game is only a few short hours, it doesn't bog itself down or drag itself out. So. The graphics are colorful, the music is fantastic, and it plays great. It covers all the bases well. Buy it. If you're fan of classic Metroid action/exploration, you owe it to yourself to get this.

title: Yooka-Laylee
text: Huge, empty worlds that are gorgeous and exciting to explore for the first time, but are painfully tedious to scour for the last few collectables? Only 5 worlds and a hub, but they’re all unnecessarily massive? A bunch of annoying physics puzzles, racing challenges, and timers? Hidden bonus challenges that make you want to tear your hair out? Wait a minute, this isn’t Banjo-Kazooie. This is Super Mario Sunshine! Seriously, Yooka-Laylee makes more sense when you look at it as a successor to Sunshine, a game that got just about as much hate as it got love. Like Sunshine, I feel that Yooka-Laylee simultaneously deserves all the love it gets, but also all the hate it gets. I haven’t felt so perfectly ambivalent over a game in a very long time. I had a lot of fun with this game, hence the thumbs-up, but I can perfectly understand why some people don’t like it. If you had a love/hate relationship with Sunshine, you can probably expect to feel exactly the same about Yooka-Laylee. For starters, the game makes a good first impression. The worlds look beautiful, the controls feel solid, and the character designs are hilariously awkward, true-to-form Rareware designs. The music is fantastic, when one of the David Wise tracks comes on. The jibberish speech and the constant barrage of fourth wall-breaking jokes and surprising double entendres often got a chuckle from me (although I have a feeling you’re going to like the jokes exactly as much as you like the game as a whole – the same way that you only really like a person’s jokes if you like that person). I felt that the best part of the game was the magical feeling of diving into a fresh new world full of details and quills and pagie challenges, and spending about an hour jumping on every rock, swimming in every puddle, getting lost and exploring every corner of the world. It was also fun to purchase all the world’s moves as soon as possible to see what they could do. While the game is far from being a Banjo-Kazooie clone, I felt it succeeded in evoking that “bring me the horizon” feel that a collect-a-thon should. But that initial impression wears off, leaving you with quite a bit of tedium to go through. To be fair, I define a challenge as something that’s unfun to play, but fun to win, and I feel that games have every right to be frustrating, annoying, obtuse, grindy, or intentionally trolling, as long as it feels great to finally win the prize in the end. I don’t feel that games need to value your time at every second of the experience -- sometimes the initiative is supposed to come from the player to play the game, and that's fine. With that out of the way, I’ll be blunt: there are several points where this game wants to frustrate you on purpose, and it doesn’t apologize for it. At every turn you’ve got unfairly hidden secrets, memorization-based bosses, annoying obstacle courses with tight timers, dead-ends, puzzles that don’t explain themselves, trivia quizzes, and slippery slopes that’ll send you careening into the pit. While this isn’t a Kaizo-style game by any means, it is a very trolling game that doesn’t always value your time. And that’s perfectly fine – as long as you’re in the mood for this kind of game. If you’re the kind of gamer that likes to conquer annoying challenges and laugh in their faces (and I’m not kidding, in this game has a face), you may just love overcoming this game’s challenges. But if you feel offended that your time is being wasted, you’ll probably hate it. It’s totally subjective, and at several points during play I flip-flopped between the two mindsets repeatedly, so I understand both sides. As far as complaints go, I suppose the biggest problem I had with the game was how hollow and samey it felt after a while. The worlds are colorful and polished, but after a while I couldn’t shake the feeling that they were just Unity sandboxes. Very detailed and pretty sandboxes, granted, but they sorely lack a dynamic feel; it doesn’t feel like your progress is doing anything besides making quills and pagies disappear from the map. Every world checks off a few boxes: One boss, 5 ghostwriters, 200 quills, one arcade machine, one minecart ride, one pagie requiring you to find several characters who are standing around, one pagie requiring you to take a grand tour of the world through Superman 64-style rings, at least one race through Superman 64-style rings, one or two pagies you can only get using a transformation, a few pagies requiring you to climb to the top of something, a few pagies requiring you to hit buttons, usually on a time limit, a few pagies that require you to find and use a nearby berry bush or edible object… and honestly, little else. There are only about 5 types of enemies in the game, too. This game could have done with a dose of more variety. A dose. But I get the feeling that a lot of planned content was cut to get the game released faster, so I guess I’ll just save my hopes for a sequel. Subjective complaints aside, I have a few mechanical criticisms with the game: * While I didn’t mind the difficulty of the game’s boss fights, they give almost zero tactile feedback when they take damage, so it’s hard to tell if you’re even doing damage or progressing the fight. They really need that Zelda-esque red flashing effect. * There are some areas of the game that force a fixed camera. If you fly into these areas, steering accurately becomes almost impossible. They added a free camera option in the latest patch, but then you have to completely control every aspect of the camera at all times, and that’s a bit more trouble than it’s worth. Personally I think they should have just disabled the fixed camera if you're flying. * In a lot of places, the clipping needs some serious work. Like in that one room in world 5 where you have to fix the pipes – they didn’t even . * The FOV is a bit too high. I’m guessing they did this to make the far-off distances look a bit farther away, adding to the illusion that the worlds are huge, but the ever-so-slight tunnel vision distortion makes it hard to judge distances when platforming. * The flight power. Is it fun? Hell yes, but it also renders all the other powers obsolete, except those required by specific Metroidvania-style barriers. It also lets you cheese almost all of the platforming puzzles, which honestly felt like cheating, especially in parts like the Rampo boss or the dark cave in world 2. If you beat the challenges before getting flight, you feel like a fool, and if you beat them after getting flight, you feel like you cheated. There’s no even medium that feels satisfying. Overall, while it’s not a good Banjo-Kazooie successor, I can’t deny that it managed to capture of its magic (and some of Super Mario Sunshine’s magic, for that matter). I enjoyed taking in the aesthetics of the wide polished worlds, and I enjoyed the satisfaction of conquering the game’s stupid challenges, of getting trolled and trolling the game back. I personally had a 7 / 10 experience, but don’t take my word for it – this is a polarizing game, you may really like it or really hate it, but definitely try it out if you're hungering for a Nintendo-styled collect-a-thon and form your own opinion. While I’m personally not eager to play the game again anytime soon, I’m definitely looking forward to a bigger, more varied sequel if one might ever be feasible. (Achievement hunters can expect to get 100% in as little as 15 hours, or as much as 40, depending on how much you want to use a guide. Most everything in this game is fundamentally easy, the problems are knowing where to find stuff and knowing which power to use.)

title: Yooka-Laylee
text: While I have many problems with this game, I don't think it's as bad as people on the internet act like it is. First off, aside from aiming with a power, the controls in the game are actually pretty good. It’s just that about every interaction with the game feels sloppy; for example, it was common for enemies to hit you even though you’re in the middle of an attack animation at them (felt like they’d go through your attack randomly), everything you can use your tongue on feels vague and random (what I mean is, the required distance and what your tongue will actually go for is mostly beyond your control if objects are somewhat close together), it seems oddly hard to just move in a straight line and you end up commonly moving in a curvy zig-zag motion constantly correcting yourself (you eventually get used to it, but it’s very weird getting to grips with it when it isn’t a problem for me in any other game), as well as other smaller things. The mini games are all a mixed bag ranging between horrible to okay and should have had much more time put on them (not that the mini games in Banjo-Tooie were much better). And the level design is also very good in places, and even does a good job at leading the player on where else to go in the level; it’s just that the things ruining that are whenever you die and whenever you move to a different area. Areas are connected at several points, though this seems like a good idea, it makes getting lost very easy to do since the transition doesn’t follow the same space logic as the areas themselves and just teleport you somewhere. Now the one level where this was fixed was in the Space world level since you can get to almost all areas without teleporting and the areas you do have to teleport  to are distinct on the outside from all the others so you don’t get it mixed up with other areas (one even, straight-up, has a sign on top of it). That’s not even mentioning how very helpful the quills are for finding new areas since they pretty much say to you that you haven’t been here yet; I just wish there was something on top of the quills (or a lot more quills meant to lead you places) because once you collect a large portion of them finding the rest will have you constantly running in circles. Of course all of that could be avoided if the levels weren’t so friggin big; which is probably what these guys like to do because I had the same problem with Banjo-Tooie back in the day (oddly enough, no one seems to point out how Tooie had this problem too but still seem to love it then complain about this game’s large levels). Aside from all of that though, everything else is great. The music is fantastic, the character design is fantastic (Trowzer is the best♥♥♥♥♥♥♥joke ever), and the story is…well charming (but the self-awareness of the characters gets a little over played). Fact is, I agree with most people, it’s mediocre. But I recommend Yooka-Laylee because it’s still very enjoyable in many places, just so long as you can get past its rougher points.

title: Yooka-Laylee
text: I'm not a fan of Banjo Kazooie and Tooie, they are a product of the 90's, they were massive collectathons with stiff animation, clunky controls and poor framerates. They also featured notoriously frustrating final boss fights which beat you down hard and had you restart the entire fight all over again. Yooka Laylee is essentially Banjo Threeie, Laylee is pretty much a dead ringer for Kazooie (personality wise). The modern graphics and powers afforded by the PC ensure a smooth experience, controls feel tight and responsive, and framerate is a silky smooth 60fps, so in that regard it is a step up from its predecessors. The graphics and presentation in atleast 4 of the 5 worlds is very Rare like, with charming oogly eyes on everything and everyone. The music is not on the same level, David Wise and Grant Kirkhope had some amazing soundtracks during the Rare SNES/N64 days, but the stuff here isnt even close to their best. Rare's classic formula is back in full swing, a couple of worlds (check), lots of jiggies (in this case, quills) and about 100 pagies needed to get to the final boss. YL features 5 worlds + 1 hub world, 4 out of the 5 worlds are actually quite good while 1 is just tedious and uninspiring (Casino world). YL follows Banjo's blue print to a T, even having the infamous death bridge quiz, where you need to get 10 answers right to advance to the next area, these are quite easy. There were times where I lost patience, wanting to finish the game as quick as possible while other moments where I was getting bored and had to push myself to reach the finish line. Hard to believe a game in 2017 doesnt have a map or fast travel. I challenged the final boss after 103 pagies, found out his pattern after a little frustration and put him out of his misery. I'd strictly only recommend this game to fans of Rare and to people who really enjoyed the Banjo games. Here's hoping the upcoming Super Mario Odyysey impresses me and shows me that there is life yet in the open world 3D platformer cause I nearly wanted to stop playing YL a few times. Better luck next time to the ex Rare team.

title: Yooka-Laylee
text: Yooka-Laylee could have been the perfect game. All of the pieces were ripe and ready to fall into place. And yet somehow the product is of lesser value than the sum of its parts. How can this possibly be? Allow me to break it down: I would like to quickly and concisely address the camera right from the get go. It can be incredibly annoying at certain points ( I recall it violently shaking during some sliding segments) but it is fine more the most part, at least in the big wide open areas (which is every area). To get more obvious points out of the way that people love to harp on: yes, the game has a very "empty" feel to it. Very large worlds with not much to fill them. It can be easy to find yourself lost once in a while. I'm already getting bored writing this review, I'm ready to put this game behind me and get it out of my brain. I won't call it utter garbage, but it really felt like a chore to finish as I was approaching my 100th pagie. And wait, I almost forgot to mention the final boss. The combat in this game is lackluster at best (I'm used to INCREDIBLY FLASHY combat I play fighting games) so you already know that the boss fights are going to be weird. Just spin your tail around a lot, mash that junk like you're playing Kingdom Hearts or something. There's a pool of acid hanging around during the final phases of the boss (this boss has too many phases) and during one of the shifts Capital B (spoilers) fell into the acid and the game soft locked. It was total BS! I was sad because I had to start the whole fight over again after that. My biggest pet peeve about the game is this: Yooka is still "active" while cutscenes are running. So for example, a cutscene is playing during an underwater sequence BUT YOU ARE STILL RUNNING OUT OF AIR EVEN THOUGH YOU HAVE NO CONTROL OF YOUR CHARACTER. So I'm watching a giant ice key unlock an underwater door and at the same time watching my character drown with no options as to what I can do to save him. I experienced the same kind of thing during the later phases of the final boss as well. He was switching from phase 3 to 4 so I had no control of Yooka but one of the boss's shockwaves was still in play and hit me so I lost a little butterfly for that. THIS IS TERRIBLE GAME DESIGN. I should not be taking damage during cutscenes. Period. I think forcing myself to slog through until the end of this game has made me insane. I am literally insane now. Thanks for reading my review.

title: Yooka-Laylee
text: I want to start this review by mentioning that I didn't play the games like Banjo Kazooie and have no nostalgia for it. World design; others may say the worlds are too big and I can see why, they are huge but I like this. Worlds are beautiful and I like the way each feels different. The challenges; I liked most of them, so e I did and I thought they could have had more to them but it was not a game ruiner for me. The bosses; 1 was kinda boring, 2 was a bit better, 3 I liked a lot, same for 4 and I enjoyed 5, THe final was kinda frustrating at first but once I remembered patterns I found the bosses enjoyable (3,4,5, Capital B). Rextros 'fun' arcade games; they weren't so bad to ruin the game, the only one I had a problem with (because it was super frustrating) was Hurdle Hijinx, it was just too long not a bad challenge. I liked the Hub World, I liked it's size and so many rooms and enjoyed moving around in it. Others have metioned the controls which some are very loose (flying) but I ghenerally felt they were tight. The characters I liked a lot. Yooka seems like cool guy who would be a nice friend and he was always patient. Laylee the Bat, she was so sassy, her interaction with the other characters was almost insulting but like friends would do, she was almost mean but not quite there. Trowzer was a big egomaniac who was just like 'I'm the best' all the time. THe other characters were pretty good but they seemed like they were a bit randomly placed sometimes. The transformations I did like minus the flower because that was slow. The humour was totally my taste, stupid bad puns, Capital B's business jokes I liked but he had something against Yooka not having clothes on, I thought this was a bit weird. In total I would probably say 7-8/10, I will look foward to a sequel and hope plauytonic will improve on the not so good parts of the game.

The game also summarizes the plot from the show for those who don't know it, and is skippable for those who don't care for it. Unfotunately, the cutscenes are just a little wooden, they need more life and spark. There is also the fact 5Ds is in it, I have no problem with it because no actual motorbike driving is involved in the gameplay (I'm terrible at driving games), but some people might. Still a solid 8/10, actually made me feel a sense of victory and nostalgia. But I am stuck on how to defeat a few specific characters.

title: Zavix Tower
text: I normally play RPG Maker games, but do play Rogue like games occassionally too. I enjoyed this game very much and have already spend 55 hours on it and am still extremely interested in the game. Let me share with you why I like this game, and what make it so captivating. Firstly, this game is fun, and can be completed in short sessions. You start off with a team of 4 but should increase it to 6 as soon as possible to give you more firepower. Then, it is a matter of short and fun trips down the dungeon to get more XP and items. I believe it is the strategic approach that make the game real fun an interesting, and if you find the right approach, it will maintain your interest in the game. The way I normally play roguelike games is to go as far down the dungeon as I can. However, this approach is not really effective with this  game, because when you die, you lose all the items that you are carrying in your inventory, and the items equipped on your dead character. Hence I have to take a totally different approach when playing this game with the goal of NOT dying. The way that this game is setup involves a boss guarding the stairs on every 5 levels. Usually these bosses are difficult if you are not fully prepared. You can leave the dungeon and go all the way back to town anytime you from ANY level once you find a stair. However, you can enter the dungeon at intervals of every 5 levels once you defeat the boss and find the stairs too. So, to prevent unnecessary deaths, I do not face the bosses until I am fully prepared. I make short trips of 1 or 2 levels to gain more XP and upgrade better gears. I also make use of the facilities in town to Enchant or Fuse gears to get good items. Furthermore, I also farm for Epic Gears, which are the best in the game. Only when I feel that I can kill all the monsters easily, then I approach and kill the bosses guarding every 5 levels. So with this strategy, I have not died once, and have got down to level 30, killing 6 bosses, and got about 25 epic gears in the process. Like I say, the fun in this game is making short trips, gaining more fighting power, and making sure that your characters do not die. I have experiemented with many different party setups but found this party of 6 extremely effective: === 2 paladins, 2 mages, 1 cleric, 1 warrior. === With this setup, you can have 3 tanks (2 paladins+warrior), 3 healers (2 paladins+cleric) and 3 strong casters (2 mages+cleric). Boss fights can be extremely tough and you definitely need 3 tanks in front and 3 dedicated healers to keep your party alive. Furthermore, the casters are the one that does the most damages with their AOEs that can wipe out an entire battlefield of monsters. So, far I am only half way done with the game (killed 6 out of 10 bosses) but I know  that I will be having many more hours of fun with this game!! I will give another update later when I finish the game too. I highly recommend this game to anyone who like to play in burst of short, fun-filled game sessions

This game looks and feels like a freemium mobile game, (albiet one that rips off WoW's art style,) but the mindless repetitive gameplay is far less of an asset to a full PC game where the game needs to sustain your full, undivided attention. Story is essentially non-existant at this point with big "coming soon" signs, but given the genre, the story is typically an excuse plot, anyway.  You're four random strangers that met at a bar and are killing bigger and bigger orcs for their pies and loot with a slightly higher +something. You start with 4 heroes of 4 classes, and you know exactly what four, because they're the same D&D started off with.  You will find absolutely nothing of interest in chracter-building (they are only now even working on having the ability to name your new characters "by popular request") or in combat, which mostly amounts to spamming the basic attacks or the one skill you upgraded to max mindlessly. Skills are purchased for gold, but "talent points" are used to upgrade skills, although the interface for this is (apparently intentionally) terribly uninformative. Given the nature of the game, you pretty much pick one skill you like and max it out.  With one talent point per level and 5 linearly-improving points to sink into each talent, you basically only make a real choice every 5 levels since this sort of game gives zero incentive not to min-max.  Respecing used to cost money or take "quests" but now just takes "quests". "Quests" in this game are arbitrary things that pop up as you enter the dungeon.  (I'm not sure if I'd praise it for streamlining the process if they weren't going to make quest choice meaningful or not, but I'm sure quest givers are "coming soon" as well.) Given the limited number of ways you can interact with this dungeon, and how you have almost no control over what you fight, the "quests" basically amount to "kill the things you were going to kill anyway, and you'll get some of the special game currency from back when this was freemium". Loot is pretty much straight Diablo-style.  Common drops have base stats for a given tier, but color-coded uncommons, rares, and yes, even purple "epic" equipment have additional bonuses to random stats. Dungeons are just a bunch of random square rooms that eventually lead to a stairwell up which, in sheer game logic, gives you the option to exit, as well.  The game claims it has "roguelike" mechanics, but all it really has is procedural dungeon layouts, and even that is moot because dungeons are so featureless that they might as well be drawing "encounters" from a deck of cards, and do away with the concept of space, entirely. In essence, there's nothing here other games at this price point don't do better.  Look at these other games, which have every feature this game has, plus have more innovative features, plus better game balance, are around the same price, and are old enough to go on sale and be cheaper (Paper Sorcerer is $5 even before a sale, and a far more deep game!): Or go for , which realized its rut and actually tried to reinvent itself to a fair degree of success. For that matter, get a DS or a Vita, and play the dozens of Wizardry clones like the Etrian Odyssey series (at least, past the first game...) or the like where at least being mindless and repetitive is an advantage on a mobile device.

title: Zigfrak
text: I can't recommend Zigrafk in its current form, but it's a great idea. Why not bring the loot-filled fun of "Torchlight" or "Borderlands" to the space-sim genre? The notion is brilliant, because it can, in theory, speed up the "go on missions, upgrade your ride" loop to a lightning pace. (And it can also create some very zany ship loadouts.) The problem here is not the lack of a novel idea. No, the problem is the execution of the flying and fighting. Zigfrak delivers a disappointing experience on those fronts, with strange ship handling and uninspired "dogfight" mechanics. There's also the problem of all the HUD displays that pop onto the screen, covering a huge amount of visual real-estate with what amounts to database entries. These elements, as drivers of the wider loot mechanic, have to be a lot of fun...but they aren't yet. They feel like they didn't get very much attention. What I would love to see Entheogen do would be to mod a game that already has fun combat and flight mechanics. A specialized loot installation, modification, and crafting mechanic could be built for stations and planets, making that part of the game a focused experience all on its own. The problem with a negative critique is that you're essentially shooting down somebody's hard work. I especially hate to do that with something like this, which tries to go in a bold direction. The developers have come up with an underlying concept that I really want to play - it's just that the actual playing isn't engaging.

text: I'd give it a 6.5. The items and their descriptions can be hilarious.  For instance, you start out with a "dusty cannon" and it's got "a colony of bunnies live inside." I also like the ability to thrust and slide in three dimensional space. That said, I do have a problem with the interface. For instance, the inventory menu.  I suppose the easiest way to explain it is that It's really compact.  All you have to distinguish the different weapon icons is the border.  Brown/Green/Blue/Purple...etc.  Unlike other rpg games where different items may have different icons, here you find that all cannons look the same.  All pulse cannons look the same.  Etc.  I have to mouse over each item just to see what it is. That wouldn't be so bad...except the game sorts everything for you.  I'm a messy guy, so I subscribe to the school of controlled chaos.  I'm the type who would store the useful items on one side of the inventory and the junk go on the other.  That way, when I land, I know what leaves and what stays. Here...The junk and the good stuff are lumped together by category, and it also looks like by level.  Quite frankly, I'm not going to remember what order the cannons are in...so once I hit level 7 and then open up the inventory to equip that cannon that had a level 7 requirement, I end up having to mouse over each item just to find it. Did I mention that the inventory menu was compact?  Guess what? The item details end up being in a window like 1/5th the required size.  And that's important why?  It means you have to scroll.  And why do you have to scroll?  Because to equip an item, you have to go to the equip options that come AFTER the description.  Right clicking like in other games doesn't work, it just brought up the descriptions. That reminds me...it looks like there's a fuel and ammo system in this game.  After some poking around, it occurred to me that I can pull that information up by accessing my inventory and then checking the engine and each individual weapon.  I think that's how you do it.  Couldn't there have been some sort of HUD for this? I'll recommend it, because it truly does seem like an interesting game.  But this user interface could've been streamlined.
